title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After the Emperor left Moscow, life flowed on there in its usual course, and that course was so ordinary that it was hard to remember the recent days of patriotic fervor, hard to believe that Russia was really in danger and that the members of the English Club were also sons of the Fatherland, ready to sacrifice everything for it. The one thing that recalled the patriotic enthusiasm everyone had shown during the Emperor's stay was the call for contributions of men and money—a demand that, once the promises had been made, assumed a legal, official form and became unavoidable.

With the enemy's approach to Moscow, the Muscovites' view of their situation did not grow more serious but actually became more frivolous, as always happens with people who see a great danger approaching. At the approach of danger, two voices always speak with equal power in the human soul: one very reasonably tells a person to consider the nature of the danger and the means of escaping it; the other, still more reasonably, says that it is too depressing and painful to think about the danger since it is not in our power to foresee everything and avert the general course of events, and that it is therefore better to ignore what is painful until it arrives, and to think about what is pleasant. In solitude, a person generally listens to the first voice; in society, to the second. So it was now with the people of Moscow. It had been a long time since people had been as merry in Moscow as that year.

Rostopchin's broadsheets, headed by woodcuts of a tavern, a barkeeper, and a Moscow citizen named Karpushka Chigirin "who—having been a militiaman and having had a bit too much at the pub—heard that Napoleon wanted to come to Moscow, got angry, cursed the French in terrible language, came out of the tavern, and under the sign of the eagle began to address the crowd" were read and discussed, alongside the latest witty verses by Vasili Lvovich Pushkin.

In the Club's corner room, members gathered to read these broadsheets, and some enjoyed the way Karpushka mocked the French, saying: "They'll swell up on Russian cabbage, burst on our buckwheat porridge, and choke on cabbage soup. They're all dwarfs, and one peasant woman could toss three of them with a pitchfork." Others disliked the tone and called it stupid and vulgar. It was said that Rostopchin had expelled all Frenchmen and even all foreigners from Moscow, and that there had been spies and agents of Napoleon among them; but this was mainly told so as to introduce Rostopchin's witty remark on the occasion. The foreigners were deported to Nizhny by boat, and Rostopchin had told them in French: "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and don't turn it into the boat of Charon." There was talk of all the government offices having already been moved from Moscow, and to this Shinshin's quip was added—that for that alone, Moscow ought to be grateful to Napoleon. It was said that Mamonov's regiment would cost him eight hundred thousand rubles, and that Bezukhov had spent even more on his, but that the best thing about Bezukhov's gesture was that he himself was going to put on a uniform and ride at the head of his regiment without charging anything for the show.
* "Look inside yourselves; get into the boat, and take care not to make it the boat of Charon."
"You don't spare anyone," said Julie Drubetskaya as she gathered and pressed together a bunch of shredded lint with her thin, ringed fingers.
Julie was preparing to leave Moscow the next day and was hosting a farewell party.
"Bezukhov is ridiculous, but he is so kind and good-natured. What pleasure is there in being so caustic?"
"A forfeit!" cried a young man in militia uniform whom Julie called "my knight" and who was traveling with her to Nizhny.

In Julie's circle, as in many other circles in Moscow, it had been agreed that they would speak nothing but Russian, and anyone who slipped into French would pay a fine to the Committee of Voluntary Contributions.
"Another forfeit for a Gallicism," said a Russian writer who was present. "'What pleasure is there in being' is not Russian!"
"You don't spare anyone," Julie continued to the young man, ignoring the writer's remark.

"For 'caustic'—I'm guilty and I'll pay, and I'm prepared to pay again for the pleasure of telling you the truth. For Gallicisms I won't take responsibility," she said, turning to the writer. "I have neither the money nor the time, like Prince Galitsyn, to hire a tutor to teach me Russian!"

"Ah, here he is!" she added. "When one— No, no," she said to the militia officer, "you won't catch me. Speak of the sun and you see its rays!" and she smiled charmingly at Pierre. "We were just talking about you," she said with the easy dishonesty natural to a society woman. "We were saying your regiment would certainly be better than Mamonov's."
"Oh, don't talk to me about my regiment," replied Pierre, kissing his hostess's hand and taking a seat beside her. "I'm so sick of it."
"You will, of course, command it yourself?" said Julie, directing a sly, sarcastic glance at the militia officer.

The latter, in Pierre's presence, had stopped being sarcastic, and his face expressed confusion about what Julie's smile might mean. Despite his absentmindedness and good nature, Pierre's personality immediately checked any attempt to ridicule him to his face.
"No," said Pierre, with a laughing glance at his large, stout body. "I'd make too easy a target for the French. Besides, I doubt I could even climb onto a horse."
Among the people Julie's guests happened to gossip about were the Rostovs.

"I hear their affairs are in very bad shape," said Julie. "And he is so unreasonable, the count himself, I mean. The Razumovskis wanted to buy his house and his estate near Moscow, but it just drags on and on. He asks too much."
"No, I think the sale will go through in a few days," said someone. "Though it's madness to buy anything in Moscow now."
"Why?" asked Julie. "You don't think Moscow is in danger?"
"Then why are you leaving?"
"Me? What a question! I'm leaving because... well, because everyone is leaving; and besides, I'm not Joan of Arc or an Amazon."
"Well, of course, of course! Let me have some more strips of linen."
"If he manages the business properly, he should be able to pay off all his debts," said the militia officer, speaking of Rostov.

"A kindly old man but not very capable. And why are they staying on so long in Moscow? They meant to leave for the country ages ago. Natalie is quite well again now, isn't she?" Julie asked Pierre with a knowing smile.

"They're waiting for their younger son," Pierre replied. "He joined Obolensky's Cossacks and was sent to Belaya Tserkov where the regiment is being formed. But now they've had him transferred to my regiment and they're expecting him any day. The count wanted to leave long ago, but the countess absolutely won't leave Moscow until her son arrives."
"I saw them the day before yesterday at the Arkharovs'. Natalie has gotten her looks back and is more cheerful. She sang a song. How easily some people get over things!"
"Get over what?" asked Pierre, looking displeased.
Julie smiled.
"You know, Count, knights like you are only found in Madame de Souza's novels."
"What knights? What do you mean?" demanded Pierre, blushing.
"Oh, come, my dear count! It's the talk of all Moscow. I admire you, I truly do!"
* "It's the talk of all Moscow. My word, I admire you!"
"Forfeit, forfeit!" cried the militia officer.
"All right, one can't say anything—how tiresome!"
"What is 'the talk of all Moscow'?" Pierre asked angrily, rising to his feet.
"Come now, Count, you know!"
"I don't know anything about it," said Pierre.
"I know you were friends with Natalie, and so... but I was always closer to Vera—that dear Vera."

"No, madame!" Pierre continued in a tone of displeasure. "I have not taken on the role of Natalie Rostova's knight at all, and haven't visited them for nearly a month. But I cannot understand the cruelty..."

"He who excuses himself, accuses himself," said Julie, smiling and waving the lint triumphantly, and to have the last word she quickly changed the subject. "Do you know what I heard today? Poor Mary Bolkonskaya arrived in Moscow yesterday. Did you know she lost her father?"
* "He who excuses himself, accuses himself."
"Really? Where is she? I would very much like to see her," said Pierre.
"I spent the evening with her yesterday. She's going to their estate near Moscow either today or tomorrow morning, with her nephew."
"Well, how is she?" asked Pierre.

"She's all right, but sad. But do you know who rescued her? It's quite a romance. Nicholas Rostov! She was surrounded, they wanted to kill her and had wounded some of her people. He rushed in and saved her..."
"Another romance," said the militia officer. "Really, this general exodus has been arranged to get all the old maids married off. Catiche is one and Princess Bolkonskaya another."
"Do you know, I actually think she's a tiny bit in love with the young man."
* "A little bit in love with the young man."
"Forfeit, forfeit, forfeit!"
"But how would you say that in Russian?"
